entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 42 Is 42:1-25 . Messiah the Antitype of Cyrus. God's description of His character ( Is 42:1-4 ). God addresses Him directly ( Is 42:5-7 ). Address to the people to attend to the subject ( Is 42:8 , 9 ). Call to all, and especially the exile Jews to rejoice in the coming deliverance ( Is 42:10-25 ). 1. my servant-- The law of prophetic suggestion leads Isaiah from Cyrus to the far greater Deliverer, behind whom the former is lost sight of. The express quotation in Mt 12:18-20 , and the description can apply to Messiah alone ( Psa 40:6 ; with which compare Ex 21:6 ; Joh 6:38 ; Php 2:7 ). Israel, also, in its highest ideal, is called the "servant" of God ( Is 49:3 ). But this ideal is realized only in the antitypical Israel, its representative-man and Head, Messiah (compare Mt 2:15 , with Ho 11:1 ). "Servant" was the position assumed by the Son of God throughout His humiliation. elect-- chosen by God before the foundation of the world for an atonement ( 1Pe 1:20 ; Re 13:8 ). Redemption was no afterthought to remedy an unforeseen evil ( Ro 16:25 , 26 ; Ep 3:9 , 11 ; 2Ti 1:9 , 10 ; Tit 1:2 , 3 ). In Mt 12:18 it is rendered "My beloved"; the only beloved Son, beloved in a sense distinct from all others. Election and the love of God are inseparably joined. soul-- a human phrase applied to God, because of the intended union of humanity with the Divinity: "I Myself." delighteth-- is well pleased with, and accepts, as a propitiation. God could have "delighted" in no created being as a mediator (compare Is 42:21 ; 63:5 ; Mt 3:17 ). spirit upon him-- ( Is 11:2 ; 61:1 ; Lu 4:18 ; Joh 3:34 ). judgment-- the gospel dispensation, founded on justice, the canon of the divine rule and principle of judgment called "the law" ( Is 2:3 ; compare Is 42:4 ; 51:4 ; 49:6 ). The Gospel has a discriminating judicial effect: saving to penitents; condemnatory to Satan, the enemy ( Joh 12:31 ; 16:11 ), and the wilfully impenitent ( Joh 9:39 ). Mt 12:18 has, "He shall show," for "He shall bring forth," or "cause to go forth." Christ both produced and announced His "judgment." The Hebrew dwells most on His producing it; Matthew on His announcement of it: the two are joined in Him.

As <reference osisRef="Isa.42.2">Is 42:2</reference> described His unturbulent spirit towards His violent enemies (<reference osisRef="Matt.12.14-Matt.12.16">Mt 12:14-16</reference>), and His utter freedom from love of notoriety, so <reference osisRef="Isa.42.3">Is 42:3</reference>, His tenderness in cherishing the first spark of grace in the penitent (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.11">Is 40:11</reference>).<div eID="gen15420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15421" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reed--</hi>fragile: easily "shaken with the wind" (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.7">Mt 11:7</reference>). Those who are at best feeble, and who besides are oppressed by calamity or by the sense of sin.<div eID="gen15421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15422" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">break--</hi>entirely crush or condemn. Compare "bind up the broken-hearted" (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.4">Is 50:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1">61:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>).<div eID="gen15422" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15423" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flax--</hi>put for the lamp-wick, formed of flax. The believer is the lamp (so the Greek, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.15">Mt 5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.35">Joh 5:35</reference>): his conscience enlightened by the Holy Ghost is the wick. "Smoking" means "dimly burning," "smouldering," the flame not quite extinct. This expresses the positive side of the penitent's religion; as "bruised reed," the negative. Broken-hearted in himself, but not without some spark of flame: literally, "from above." Christ will supply such a one with grace as with oil. Also, the light of nature smouldering in the Gentiles amidst the hurtful fumes of error. He not only did not quench, but cleared away the mists and superadded the light of revelation. See Jerome, To Algasia, Question 2.<div eID="gen15423" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15424" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">truth--</hi><reference osisRef="Matt.12.20">Mt 12:20</reference> quotes it, "send forth judgment unto victory." Matthew, under the Spirit, gives the virtual sense, but varies the word, in order to bring out a fresh aspect of the same thing. Truth has in itself the elements of victory over all opposing forces. Truth is the victory of Him who is "the truth" (<reference osisRef="John.14.6">Joh 14:6</reference>). The gospel judicial sifting ("judgment") of believers and unbelievers, begun already in part (<reference osisRef="John.3.18">Joh 3:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.3.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.9.39">9:39</reference>), will be consummated victoriously in truth only at His second coming; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Is 42:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.42.14">14</reference>, here, and <reference osisRef="Matt.12.32">Mt 12:32</reference>, 36, 41, 42, show that there is reference to the judicial aspect of the Gospel, especially finally: besides the mild triumph of Jesus coming in mercy to the penitent now (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.2">Is 42:2</reference>), there shall be finally the judgment on His enemies, when the "truth" shall be perfectly developed. Compare <reference osisRef="Isa.61.1-Isa.61.3">Is 61:1-3</reference>, where the two comings are similarly joined (Psa 2:4-6, 8; <reference osisRef="Rev.15.2">Re 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.15.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.19.11-Rev.19.16">19:11-16</reference>). On "judgment," see on <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>. <div eID="gen15424" type="x-p"/>

Mt 12:21 virtually gives the sense, with the inspired addition of another aspect of the same thing, "In his name shall the Gentiles trust" (as "wait for" here means, Is 30:18 ). "His law" is not something distinct from Himself, but is indeed Himself, the manifestation of God's character ("name") in Christ, who is the embodiment of the law ( Is 42:21 ; Jr 23:6 ; Ro 10:4 ). "Isles" here, and in Is 42:12 , may refer to the fact that the populations of which the Church was primarily formed were Gentiles of the countries bordering on the Mediterranean.

"Opening ... ears," that is, though he (Israel) hath his ears open (see on Is 6:10 ). This language, too (see on Is 42:19 ), applies to Messiah as Jehovah's servant ( Is 50:5 ; Psa 40:6 ).

God is well pleased with His Son ("in whom My soul delighteth," <reference osisRef="Isa.42.1">Is 42:1</reference>), "who fulfils all righteousness" (<reference osisRef="Matt.3.15">Mt 3:15</reference>) for them, and with them for His sake (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.42.6">Is 42:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.16">Psa 71:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.71.19">19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.5.17">Mt 5:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.10.3">Ro 10:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.4">4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.3.9">Php 3:9</reference>).
